segments.text: Take that curve in the photograph and straighten it in your mind. You could travel from the clear end to the pink end without ever crossing open water. That connection matters. A school of fish can make one shape, too. When the school splits, each fish takes its own engine and its own mouth with it.

A siphonophore starts small, from a single fertilized egg. As it grows, new individuals bud from tissue that's already there. They keep the connection. Imagine drawing its family tree on transparent paper, then laying the drawing over the living animal. In places, the family tree would still be physically joined.

In the swimming region, one of those individuals becomes a bell. It can change shape, push water, and help move its neighbors. Look for a mouth on that swimmer and you'll be looking in the wrong place. Farther along, a feeding individual can take in a meal that a swimmer never could.

Now try to steer the colony. You have several jets pointing away from a slender body. You want to turn left without rolling the whole thing over. Would you fire the strongest bell first? A study of a siphonophore called Nanomia found a surprisingly good reason to start with the small ones.

This image comes from the researchers who investigated how Nanomia swims. Look along the swimming region. The youngest bells sit near the tip. Farther back are larger, older bells. Age changes more than how much water a bell can expel. It changes where the push lands on the colony.

Picture a door that's standing a little open. Press close to its hinge, then press just as gently at the handle. Your hand supplies the same push, but the second push turns the door more easily. In the water there's no fixed hinge. The useful part of that comparison is the distance from the point you're turning around.

The young bells near the front have leverage. Even a modest jet there can turn Nanomia. Older bells closer to the base of the swimming region contribute more to forward thrust. Now watch the diagram again. First the nose changes direction. Then the larger bells help carry the feeding region onto the new heading.

There's another trick inside a single stroke. Researchers filmed several species swimming and compared neighboring bells frame by frame. On one side, the pulses could follow one another in a wave. Across the two sides, they didn't see the same lockstep timing. A colony can travel together without every swimmer squeezing at the very same instant.

Keep your eye on the tentacles as the swimmer leaves the frame. They trail behind, in water the colony has just passed through. Moving a feeding apparatus into position is only half the problem. Once it's there, how does something so delicate bring a fast fish within reach?

Picture the view from a small fish in midwater. The expedition lamps go out. The great sweep of transparent tissue disappears. What remains visible might be a moving point of light, with nothing around it to reveal what's holding it. For one deep Pacific hunter, that difference is the opportunity.

Meet the angler siphonophore, Erenna sirena. The clear animal photographed off Puerto Rico at the beginning was a different observation. Here we're following a Pacific species that researchers found carrying tiny lures on the finest branches of its tentacles. The whole colony swims. The invitation to a fish comes from a much smaller piece.

Follow one tentacle in the enlarged view. Now take a branch off that branch. At the end is a lure that can twitch. A fish approaching from the darkness would encounter that little moving target before it could work out the outline of the hunter behind it. These few inches of screen stand in for a much smaller structure.

The color is a clue to how the lure works. Living tissue produces light. The researchers also found fluorescent material in the lure. It absorbs light and gives some back at a different wavelength. Put those processes together and the mature lure can send out a reddish signal. The surrounding colony doesn't have to light up.

Here's a lanternfish, the kind of small midwater fish that puts the size of this meal in perspective. Notice the eye. Now imagine its view of the lure. Scientists have suggested the twitching tip resembles a small crustacean a fish might eat. We can describe the light and the motion. What the fish takes them to mean is an inference.

That distinction changes how you watch a hunt. A glowing tip in a frame is evidence for a glowing tip. A fish found inside a feeding polyp is evidence for a meal. The tempting story in between has to fit both observations. The tentacle puts stinging cells within reach of a fish drawn toward the moving light.

Suppose you found only the bell end in a sample jar. You could work out how the colony swam, and miss almost everything about what it ate. Suppose you found only a loose tentacle. You might see the bright tip, yet never know where it hung in relation to the mouth. The arrangement itself is evidence.

This is where a remotely operated vehicle earns its place in the story. A tether connects the vehicle to a ship. The people watching the screens above can stop, turn, and look along a colony that's still suspended in water. They can record which end is pulsing before deciding where to look next.

Start the camera too close and every ripple looks like a separate jelly. Pull all the way back and the finest branches vanish. The wide view supplies an address for the close view. First locate the swimming end. Then follow the shared stem. Only then does a close pass by a tentacle tell you which part of the animal you're seeing.

The light used to see the colony changes the picture, too. Expedition lamps reveal the outline of transparent tissue as it bends and reflects their light. A lure making light of its own asks a different question. An illuminated portrait and an observation of a glow in darkness can describe the same animal while showing quite different things.

Go back to Puerto Rico. The photograph hasn't changed. Try reading it from the tip this time. There's a region built for pushing water, then a bend, then structures with a different outline. You can recognize the division of labor without assigning this animal the red lures of its Pacific relative.

So is it one hunter or many animals? Follow the development and you find individuals budding from a common beginning. Follow a turn, and one set of individuals steers while another drives. Follow a meal, and the tentacle and the mouth belong to one connected system. Count the workers and you get many. Watch the hunt and you see one colony.
